newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Battle for skies begins as Korea air show ends.
newsitem.headline: Battle for skies begins as Korea air show ends.

text.p: The first Seoul Air Show drew to a close on Sunday, but the dogfight for a piece of South Korea's multi-billion dollar air defence modernisation programme is just hotting up.
As jets roared over the Seoul City Airport tarmac to the thrill of thousands of families out for the day, exhibitors prepared to shut their booths.
"The show went better than I expected, especially for a first effort," said one European exhibitor. "I just wish next time they set aside more time for the exhibitors to meet and talk shop."

Although few major contracts were signed during the seven-day trade show, traditional U.S. suppliers had been pitted against Western European and Russian rivals for South Korea's lucrative fighter jet and air defence contracts.

The show was abuzz with speculation about who would ultimately land a chunk of Seoul's 20 trillion won ($24 billion) plan to buy or build fighter jets, surveillance planes and other defence equipment by 2010.

Top contenders for South Korea's next generation fighter jet programme, known as the FX project, are France's Dassault Aviation's Rafale, the U.S. Air Force's F-15E developed by McDonnell Douglas Corp, Russia's Sukhoi Su-35, and the Eurofighter 2000.
South Korea plans to buy 120 planes under the FX programme. These will join the 120 F-16 planes Seoul is acquiring through its Korea Fighter Programme, launched in the late 1980s.
The programme is designed to reinforce the nation's superiority over North Korea's MiG fighters.
No decision is expected to be made until at least 1997, or even later, exhibitors said.
More than 200 exhibitors from 21 nations attended the show, which cost about 7.1 billion won to stage, said Cha Chong-yol, the organising committee's co-director.
There was no government funding for the show, which was paid for by revenue from exhibitor fees, advertising and entry charges, he said.
"A show like this is important for our country because the development of the aerospace industry will be the basis of Korean advancement into the ranks of the truly developed nations," Cha said.
During the show, Samsung Aerospace Industries said it signed a deal with Northrup Grumman to supply parts for Boeing Co's 747-500 aircraft. It hoped to win around $200 million in orders.
Samsung also signed an agreement with Pratt & Whitney Canada, a unit of United Technologies Corp, to build engines for the Bell Helicopter 427 light twin-engine helicopter.
Korean Air Lines Co and Sikorsky Aircraft Corp, a unit of United Technologies Corp, also agreed to jointly invest $400 million over the next six years to develop multi-purpose helicopters.
The Seoul Airshow will be held biennally, with the next show scheduled for October 1998, organisers said. ($1 = 828 won)
